findings: 1. The solar page is effectively empty - one photograph and nothing else. This is the finding that matters most, because 56 creatives are pointing at this part of the site. Fetched live on 14 Sep 2026, crigroups.com/solar-pump/ returns a single image file (solar-panel.jpg) and no readable body content at all - no HP-wise product table, no subsidy explanation, no pricing, no case studies, no enquiry form, no downloadable spec sheet. The indexed description promises real substance ('MNRE approved PM-KUSUM models available', '1.0 HP - 3.0 HP Solar Pumping System', corrosion-resistant stainless steel, remote monitoring), so the content exists somewhere in the stack - it simply does not render for a visitor or a crawler. A farmer or a state-agency buyer arriving from an ad lands on a picture of a solar panel.

2. The Day-1 domain does not serve the brand's own site. cripumps.com resolves to crigroups.com, and the solar business is a subfolder of a 9,000-product group corporate site rather than a destination of its own. There is no dedicated CRI Solar property. So the Rs.8-20 lakh a month is buying clicks into a generic fluid-management homepage whose hero carousel rotates awards banners, a product-registration link and a 360-degree virtual experience - none of which is solar. The buyer has to self-navigate from 'world's fastest-growing fluid management solution provider' to a solar pump. Most will not.

3. There is no PM-KUSUM subsidy content anywhere - and KUSUM is the entire reason this business exists. The single most searched question from this audience is 'how much will the pump cost me after subsidy'. The answer is publicly defined and highly persuasive: 60% combined subsidy (30% central + 30% state) as standard, rising to 90% for SC/ST and Bundelkhand-priority farmers in UP, with the farmer paying only 10-40%. In rupees that turns a 3 HP pump from roughly Rs.1.2-1.5 lakh into Rs.24,000-45,000, and a 5 HP from Rs.2.5-3 lakh into roughly Rs.70,000-1.2 lakh. CRI is an MNRE-empanelled vendor and can state this with authority. It states none of it. Competitors and state-agency aggregators are ranking for exactly these queries instead.

4. The scheme has a real deadline and the funnel is not using it. On 28 March 2026 MNRE extended PM-KUSUM Phase 1 completion to 31 March 2027 for projects with PPAs or NTPs issued on or before 31 Dec 2025 - but for Component B and Component C individual pump solarisation, commissioning is due by 30 September 2026, which is roughly a fortnight from this audit. MNRE has signalled this is the final blanket relief, with further extensions case-by-case, while PM-KUSUM 2.0 remains un-notified. That is genuine, documentable urgency - the rarest asset in performance marketing - and it appears in none of the messaging. Unlike the false countdown some competitors run, this one is real and citable.

5. The best numbers in Indian solar pumping are sitting in press releases instead of creatives. 1,81,000 systems commissioned. Rs.320 crore MSEDCL empanelment for 10,714 pumps. Rs.300 crore of earlier PM-KUSUM-3 orders across four states. 6,100 million kWh saved. 4.8 million tonnes of CO2 prevented. IoT-enabled remote monitoring with a 5-year warranty. A named chairman quote from G. Soundararajan. The Day-1 leak - 'zero case-study proof in ads' - is confirmed and understated: this is not a brand that lacks references, it is a brand whose references never left the newsroom. For a state-agency tender buyer, 1,81,000 installed units is the single most decisive fact available, and for a farmer, a 5-year warranty plus IoT monitoring answers the objection that actually kills solar-pump deals: what happens when it breaks.

6. No WhatsApp, no vernacular, for an audience that is WhatsApp-first and rarely reads English. The funnel offers a Meta Lead Form and a corporate contact route. There is no WhatsApp entry point, no Tamil, Hindi or Marathi landing content, and no click-to-call sized for a farmer on a 4G phone - despite the Rs.320 crore order being in Maharashtra under the Marathi-named 'Magel Tyala Saur Krushi Pump' scheme, and despite UP and Rajasthan being the largest Component B markets. Lead-form leads from this segment also arrive without the two qualifiers that decide everything: state and HP requirement. Without those, the sales team cannot route to the right nodal-agency workflow.

7. Tracking is aimed at the wrong event, and the group site is leaking third-party scripts. With a Lead Form objective and no on-site funnel, there are no mid-funnel signals to optimise against - no subsidy-calculator start, no HP selector, no spec-sheet download, no dealer-locator search. Meta is being asked to find buyers using nothing but raw form fills, which in an agri-subsidy category is the noisiest possible signal. Separately, the group homepage attempts to load a Criteo retargeting script (gum.criteo.com) that renders a visible 'gum.criteo.com is blocked ... ERR_BLOCKED_BY_CLIENT' error block in the page body - a retargeting tag that is both failing and, when it fails, printing an error message to the customer.
